content: In the 24 hours following the administration of immediate-release ketoprofen 75 mg capsules taken three times daily (TID) for 12 hours, the accumulation of ketoprofen in the plasma is minimal relative to the peak plasma concentration. After the second 50 mg dose, there is a noticeable reduction in both the peak plasma concentration and the area under the curve (AUC). This reduction is likely influenced by a combination of factors, including the effects of food, circadian rhythms, and the timing of plasma sampling. However, the specific contribution of each factor to the observed reduction remains unclear. Ketoprofen undergoes metabolism primarily through glucuronide conjugation, forming an unstable acyl-glucuronide metabolite. The glucuronic acid moiety of this metabolite can revert to the parent compound, effectively serving as a reservoir for the active drug. This process may be particularly significant in individuals with renal insufficiency, as the conjugate can accumulate in the serum and subsequently undergo deconjugation back to the parent drug. In healthy adults, these conjugates are present only in trace amounts in plasma, but their levels are higher in elderly individuals, likely due to reduced renal clearance. Studies have shown that in elderly subjects receiving multiple doses of ketoprofen (50 mg every 6 hours), the ratio of conjugated to parent ketoprofen AUC was 30% for the S-enantiomer and 3% for the R-enantiomer. There are no known active metabolites of ketoprofen, and the drug does not induce drug-metabolizing enzymes. Approximately 80% of an administered dose of ketoprofen is excreted in the urine within 24 hours, primarily as the glucuronide metabolite. Enterohepatic recirculation of the drug has been hypothesized, but this has not been confirmed through measurement of biliary levels. In cases of slow drug absorption, the elimination rate becomes dependent on the absorption rate, which can result in a prolonged half-life (t1/2) relative to intravenous (IV) administration. In elderly individuals (mean age 73 years), both plasma and renal clearance of ketoprofen are reduced compared to younger adults (mean age 27 years). Consequently, the peak plasma concentration and AUC of ketoprofen increase with age. Additionally, the unbound fraction of the drug in plasma also increases with age, with data suggesting that this increase is more pronounced in women than in men. It remains uncertain whether age-related changes in drug absorption contribute to the altered bioavailability of ketoprofen in elderly individuals. In a study comparing young and elderly subjects, those older than 75 years exhibited a 40% increase in free drug AUC and a 60% increase in Cmax compared to younger subjects (under 35 years). Furthermore, in the elderly, the ratio of intrinsic clearance to availability decreased by 35%, and the plasma half-life was prolonged by 26%. These changes are thought to result from a decline in hepatic extraction efficiency associated with aging. The efficacy of ketoprofen has been demonstrated in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis. In clinical trials, ketoprofen showed comparable effectiveness to other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, piroxicam, diclofenac, and indomethacin. However, some studies reported a higher rate of gastrointestinal side effects leading to treatment discontinuation among patients taking ketoprofen compared to those on other NSAIDs. In rheumatoid arthritis studies, ketoprofen was used in combination with other treatments such as gold salts, antimalarials, low-dose methotrexate, D-penicillamine, and/or corticosteroids, with results comparable to those seen with control NSAIDs. The analgesic effectiveness of immediate-release ketoprofen capsules has been evaluated in standard pain models. Doses ranging from 25 mg to 150 mg were studied, with 25 mg doses proving superior to placebo. While doses higher than 25 mg did not consistently demonstrate significantly greater effectiveness, there was a trend toward faster onset and longer duration of action with 50 mg doses. In cases of dysmenorrhea, 75 mg doses showed a significantly greater overall effect. Doses exceeding 50–75 mg did not provide additional analgesic benefit. In studies of postoperative pain, ketoprofen doses of 25–100 mg were found to be comparable to 650 mg of acetaminophen combined with either 60 mg of codeine or 10 mg of oxycodone. Ketoprofen tended to have a slower onset of action, but peak pain relief was similar, and the duration of effect was 1–2 hours longer, particularly with higher doses. Ketoprofen capsules are available in the following formulation: 50 mg capsules with a blue cap and light blue body, imprinted with “93” over “3193” on both the cap and body, supplied in bottles of 100.
